course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: The Global Tapestry
unit.description: Explore how societies organized power, shared beliefs, and built their economies across the world.

topic.title: Comparisons in the Period

framework.name: InSPECT
framework.title: Use InSPECT to choose your evidence
framework.intro: A fact can connect to more than one lens. Choose the lens that helps answer the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Based on the class Early Religions + InSPECT slides, pages 5-17.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which statement makes the strongest comparison of political administration?
choices: Song rulers used exam-selected officials, while the Mexica built large temples and pyramids in Tenochtitlan
Song China grew Champa rice, while the Mexica farmed on chinampas in Lake Texcoco
Song rulers used exam-selected officials, while Mexica rulers collected tribute through local leaders
Song China and the Mexica state both existed at some point between 1200 and 1450
questions.explanation: Both halves describe the same category, how each state administered territory.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The first half is about administration, but temples are about religion, so the halves do not match.
This compares agriculture, not administration.
Both halves describe the same category, how each state administered territory.
Sharing a time period is not a comparison of administration.
questions.distinguisher: Both sides must address the same category.

questions.prompt: What is a defensible similarity between Mali and Ethiopia?
choices: Rulers drew legitimacy from religious patronage, though of different faiths
Both states were Christian kingdoms linked to the Coptic Church in Egypt
Both states depended mainly on Indian Ocean ports for their revenue
Rulers drew legitimacy from Islam, which both states adopted as their official religion
questions.explanation: Mali's rulers patronized Islam and Ethiopia's patronized Christianity; both used religion for legitimacy.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Mali's rulers patronized Islam and Ethiopia's patronized Christianity; both used religion for legitimacy.
Ethiopia was Christian; Mali's rulers were Muslim.
Mali was an inland empire tied to Saharan trade.
Mali's rulers were Muslim, but Ethiopia's were Christian.
questions.distinguisher: A similarity of function can involve different beliefs.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim that states obtained resources in different forms?
choices: Both the Mexica and Inca relied on maize and other American crops
Mexica tribute was paid in goods, and Inca subjects also paid their taxes mainly in goods
Both the Mexica and Inca built large capitals in mountainous regions
Mexica tribute was paid in goods, while Inca mit'a required labor service
questions.explanation: Goods versus labor shows two different forms of resource extraction.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Shared crops do not show different methods of extraction.
Paying goods in both cases would show a similarity, not a difference, and the Inca relied mainly on labor.
Capitals do not show how resources were collected; Tenochtitlan was in a lake basin.
Goods versus labor shows two different forms of resource extraction.
questions.distinguisher: Evidence must show the specific difference claimed.

questions.prompt: Which example illustrates continuity with innovation?
choices: Chinese dynasties kept a bureaucracy, and recruitment stayed exactly the same for centuries
Chinese dynasties kept a bureaucracy while revising how officials were recruited
The Abbasid caliphate's fall in 1258 ended Islamic institutions everywhere
Maya cities ended when their rulers adopted Christianity from Spain
questions.explanation: The bureaucratic tradition persisted while recruitment and administration changed over time.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Continuity is right, but this choice leaves out the innovation the question asks for.
The bureaucratic tradition persisted while recruitment and administration changed over time.
Islamic institutions continued in successor states after 1258.
Maya cities continued before European contact; Christianity arrived only after 1500.
questions.distinguisher: Name both what persisted and what changed.

questions.prompt: Which sentence provides the explanation in an APE response about rice and cities?
choices: Song China had large cities such as Hangzhou and Kaifeng
More food could support more people working outside farming, so towns grew
Rice was one of the main crops grown in Song China
Champa rice ripened quickly and spread across much of southern China after 1000
questions.explanation: This sentence explains how the evidence connects to the claim about urban growth.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: This states a fact about cities without linking it to rice.
This sentence explains how the evidence connects to the claim about urban growth.
This is background, not an explanation.
This is evidence (the Prove step), not the explanation linking it to cities.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly challenges the claim that all states centralized between 1200 and 1450?
choices: The Mexica built an alliance that collected tribute widely
Mali and the Inca expanded across large territories
Song China expanded its bureaucracy of scholar-officials
Maya and Hausa cities continued to have separate rulers
questions.explanation: Decentralized city-states contradict a claim that every state centralized.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: A tribute empire supports centralization.
Expansion supports centralization rather than challenging it.
A growing bureaucracy supports centralization.
Decentralized city-states contradict a claim that every state centralized.
questions.distinguisher: A challenge must contradict the claim.

questions.prompt: What chronology caution matters when comparing the Song and Inca states?
choices: The Song ended in 1279, long before the major Inca expansion after about 1438
The Song ended in 1279, shortly after the Inca had reached their largest size
The two states fought a war over Pacific trade routes in the 1300s
Both reached their greatest size in the same year, around 1350
questions.explanation: They fall in the same broad period but did not exist at their height at the same time.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: They fall in the same broad period but did not exist at their height at the same time.
The Song date is right, but the Inca's largest size came in the late 1400s.
The two states had no contact.
Their peaks were more than a century apart.
questions.distinguisher: Same period does not mean same moment.

questions.prompt: A historian uses a royal temple to claim every subject supported the ruler. What is the main weakness?
choices: Buildings cannot provide any historical evidence about the past
Temples were built after 1450, so they fall outside the period
Royal patronage does not reveal the beliefs or loyalty of every subject
Royal temples were always built by foreign architects for visiting rulers
questions.explanation: A temple shows what rulers sponsored and could mobilize, not what all subjects believed.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Buildings are valuable evidence, but of specific things, such as resources and patronage.
Many royal temples date from within this period.
A temple shows what rulers sponsored and could mobilize, not what all subjects believed.
Royal temples were usually built by local workers and artisans.
questions.distinguisher: Match the claim to what the evidence can show.

choices: Events that happened in the same year
One interesting fact about each case
The most famous ruler in each case
A shared category in two or more cases
questions.explanation: A comparison sets the same feature side by side in different cases.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Cases can be compared across a period.
Facts alone do not form a comparison without a shared category.
Fame is not a category of comparison.
A comparison sets the same feature side by side in different cases.
questions.distinguisher: Comparison starts with a shared category.

choices: The total size of a ruler's standing army
A ruler's ability to collect tribute
Accepted justification for holding authority
The number of temples a ruler built
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the belief that a ruler has the right to rule.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Military size is power, not legitimacy.
Collecting tribute shows power, which legitimacy helps justify.
Legitimacy is the belief that a ruler has the right to rule.
Temples can support legitimacy, but they are not the definition.

questions.prompt: Which InSPECT lens most directly fits required payments and labor obligations?
choices: S: Social interactions
E: Economic systems
T: Technology and innovation
P: Political systems
questions.explanation: Payments and labor obligations describe how goods and work were produced and taken.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.7 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Social rank shaped who owed labor, but the obligations are economic.
Payments and labor obligations describe how goods and work were produced and taken.
Technology concerns tools and techniques, not obligations.
Political power enforced these obligations, but the payments are economic.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two passages?
choices: Song China collected obligations in labor, while the Inca collected coin
Song China used written records, while the Inca used no records at all
Song China used written records, while the Inca used knotted cords
Song China relied on local hereditary leaders, while the Inca relied on rotating officials
questions.explanation: Passage A mentions written records; Passage B says Inca obligations were recorded on knotted cords.
choiceExplanations: This also reverses them: the Inca counted obligations in work, while the Song taxed grain, cloth, and coin.
Passage B says the Inca kept records with knotted cords, so they did have records.
Passage A mentions written records; Passage B says Inca obligations were recorded on knotted cords.
This reverses the passages: the Song rotated officials, while the Inca used local kurakas.
questions.distinguisher: The Inca had no alphabetic writing, but Passage B says they recorded obligations on knotted cords.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.7, KC-3.2.I.A and KC-3.2.I.D.i: comparison of state formation in Song China and the Inca Empire
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage A written for Page One, describing how Song China governed its territory
stimulusBlocks.text: Passage A: Song China governed tens of millions of people through a salaried bureaucracy. Officials, most of them selected through examinations, were rotated between posts so that they would not build local power bases. Taxes were paid in grain, cloth, and increasingly in coin, and written records tracked land and households.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.7, KC-3.2.I.A and KC-3.2.I.D.i: comparison of state formation in Song China and the Inca Empire
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage B written for Page One, describing how the Inca Empire governed its territory
stimulusBlocks.text: Passage B: The Inca ruled several million people across the Andes. Members of the Inca nobility held the highest posts, while local leaders called kurakas kept authority over their own communities as long as they delivered the labor the state demanded. Obligations were counted in work rather than coin and were recorded on knotted cords instead of in writing.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a similarity between the states in the two passages?
choices: Both used systems for tracking the obligations of subjects
Both relied mainly on merchants to collect taxes
Both selected officials from the hereditary nobility only
Both selected officials through written examinations
questions.explanation: Song written records and Inca knotted cords both tracked what subjects owed the state.
choiceExplanations: Song written records and Inca knotted cords both tracked what subjects owed the state.
Neither passage describes merchants collecting taxes.
Song officials were selected mostly through examinations, not by birth.
Only the Song used examinations.
questions.distinguisher: The Inca filled high posts from their nobility, but Song officials were mostly chosen by examination.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims would best use both passages as evidence?
choices: Large states could only be governed by officials who could read and write
Large states always replaced local leaders with officials sent out from the capital city
Large states developed similar tax systems based on coin
Large states developed different methods to organize and record what subjects owed

The Inca kept local leaders in place.
The Inca counted obligations in work, not coin.

questions.prompt: The passage best supports which of the following comparisons?
choices: Rulers of different faiths rejected support for religious institutions
Rulers of different faiths used religious patronage to strengthen their authority
Rulers of different faiths required all subjects to adopt the ruler's religion
Rulers of the same faith formed alliances across Africa and Asia
questions.explanation: Muslim, Hindu, and Christian rulers all supported religious institutions to tie their rule to faith.
choiceExplanations: Each ruler supported religious institutions; none rejected them.
Muslim, Hindu, and Christian rulers all supported religious institutions to tie their rule to faith.
The passage says many subjects continued older local practices.
The three rulers followed different religions, and the passage describes no alliance.
questions.distinguisher: Patronage linked rulers to religion, but the passage notes that many subjects kept older practices.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.7, KC-3.2.I: comparison of how rulers used religion to legitimize state power, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, comparing religion and royal authority in three states, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
Rulers in many regions linked their authority to religion. Mansa Musa of Mali publicized his Muslim faith through his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and sponsored mosques in Timbuktu. Vijayanagara kings endowed great Hindu temples. Ethiopia's Solomonic kings, who took power in 1270, claimed descent from the biblical King Solomon and supported Christian monasteries.

In each case, religious patronage did more than express personal belief. It tied rulers to respected institutions and to networks of scholars and clergy, though many subjects continued older local practices.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be most useful in explaining the Solomonic kings' claim of descent from King Solomon?
choices: Portuguese explorers who reached Ethiopia in the 1500s
Ethiopian traditions connecting the royal line to biblical history
Muslim scholars in Timbuktu who wrote histories of Mali
Ethiopian traditions connecting the royal line to the Prophet Muhammad
questions.explanation: Ethiopian tradition linked the dynasty to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, rooting royal authority in Christian scripture.
choiceExplanations: The Portuguese arrived long after the claim was established in 1270.
Ethiopian tradition linked the dynasty to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, rooting royal authority in Christian scripture.
Timbuktu's scholars wrote about West Africa, not Ethiopian kingship.
The Solomonic claim was biblical, not Islamic.
questions.distinguisher: The claim did rest on Ethiopian tradition, but on biblical Solomon, not on the Prophet Muhammad.

questions.prompt: Which of the following examples from the passage best illustrates continuity?
choices: The rapid creation of the Inca Empire
Turkic elites founding new sultanates in India
Turkic elites replacing Abbasid authority
Song officials using long-standing Confucian ideas
questions.explanation: Using ideas more than a thousand years old shows continuity.
choiceExplanations: A new empire built within a century is an example of change.
A new sultanate represents a change in political power.
New rulers replacing old ones is an example of change.
Using ideas more than a thousand years old shows continuity.
questions.distinguisher: Founding a new sultanate is a change in who rules, even if the rulers kept Islamic traditions.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.7, KC-3.2: continuity and change in state formation, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing continuity and change in states, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
Many states of this period built on older foundations. Song officials used Confucian ideas that were more than a thousand years old, and Ethiopian kings drew on a Christian tradition dating back to Aksum. At the same time, new forms of rule appeared. Turkic military elites replaced Abbasid authority across much of Dar al-Islam, and the Inca created one of the largest empires in the world within about a century.

Historians therefore describe the period as one in which states reused inherited ideas and institutions while adapting them to new circumstances.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the author's overall argument?
choices: States in this period adapted inherited ideas while creating new institutions
States in this period were shaped mainly by contact with Europe
States in this period preserved their earlier traditions and institutions without real change
States in this period broke completely with earlier traditions
questions.explanation: The conclusion says states reused inherited ideas and institutions while adapting them.
choiceExplanations: The conclusion says states reused inherited ideas and institutions while adapting them.
The passage does not discuss European contact as a cause.
The passage gives several examples of new forms of rule.
The passage stresses that many states built on older foundations.
questions.distinguisher: Inherited ideas mattered, but the passage also stresses new forms of rule such as Turkic sultanates and the Inca Empire.
